newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope meets Poland's ex-communist president.
newsitem.headline: Pope meets Poland's ex-communist president.

text.p: Pope John Paul met Poland's ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski for the first time on Monday amid strains in relations between the Roman Catholic Church and state in his homeland.

The Polish Pontiff, who was a key force behind the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe and is a close friend and confidant of former president Lech Walesa, held 40 minutes of talks with Kwasniewski at the Vatican.
Though the audience was billed as private, Kwasniewski was granted some of the privileges usually reserved for statesmen on official visits, including an honour guard by the Swiss Guard.

The two men exchanged polite handshakes at the start of the audience, though the atmosphere appeared warmer when Kwasniewski introduced his wife Yolanta, daughter Aleksandra and other members of his entourage to the Pope after their private talks.

"When I come to Poland, you'll have a lot to do with me," the Pope told Kwasniewski in a reference to his planned 11-day trip starting on May 31. "I'll cause you a lot of problems," he added in a quip about security and other organisational aspects.
Kwasniewski replied that Poland would be ready.
The Vatican had no immediate comment on the talks and Kwasniewski was holding a news conference later.

Relations between Warsaw and the Vatican have been clouded by a liberalised abortion law, which Kwasniewski signed last year despite protests from the Pope, and delays to ratification of a concordat treaty between Poland and the Vatican.
Kwasniewski's ex-communist colleagues from the ruling leftist coalition have been blocking ratification of the treaty, which keeps the state and the church separate.

"I think conditions have now emerged for opponents of the concordat to reconsider their views," Kwasniewski told reporters in Warsaw before his departure, adding he would discuss developments with the Pope.

Kwasniewski met his political allies from the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) on Friday to convince them that the concordat could be ratified after the recent passage of a new constitution.

He said that the SLD, which opposes the concordat on grounds that it would give the Catholic Church too much influence over life in Poland, could now be more willing to back the treaty before parliamentary elections due around September.
The concordat was signed in 1993 by the then right-centrist, pro-Church government, just before the ex-communists and a peasant party won parliamentary elections.
The Pontiff is widely believed to have provided much of the spiritual inspiration for Walesa's Solidarity movement to overthrow communism in 1989.
Many analysts say the Pope's visit to Poland is likely to boost the chances of rightist parties in the coming elections.
